performers: Hochschulsymphonieorchester, University of Music and Theatre Munich; Marcus Bosch, conductor
intro: The Adagio of Bruckner’s Symphony No. 7 in E major, WAB 107, marked Sehr feierlich und sehr langsam, opens with a C♯-minor melody for four Wagner tubas. Bruckner built this melody to a climax in C major, and the movement has a quiet ending for violins and low brass.

sections.label: A · Wagner tubas in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: Low strings double the brass; violins follow on the G string.

sections.label: Link · Clarinet and tubas without strings
sections.mNote: Brass chords follow the clarinet’s descending phrase.

sections.label: B · String theme in F♯ major, Moderato
sections.mNote: Moderato, in triple time; the violins play a flowing melody.

sections.label: A′ · Tubas return, moving string figuration
sections.mNote: The opening C♯-minor melody returns with a new violin line.

sections.label: B′ · String theme returns in A♭
sections.mNote: Flute, oboe and bassoon join the returning Moderato melody.

sections.label: A″ · Tubas beneath even violin arpeggios
sections.mNote: The opening theme returns a third time, very slowly

sections.label: C · Brass and strings in C major
sections.mNote: Broad wind and brass phrases above running violins

sections.label: Link · Plucked violins, then tubas
sections.mNote: The strings stop before the low brass begin alone.

sections.label: Coda · Violins after the low brass
sections.mNote: String and wind phrases lead to the final chorale.

cues.title: Opening, Wagner tubas and contrabass tuba
cues.text: Four Wagner tubas and a contrabass tuba begin in C♯ minor, doubled by violas, cellos and basses. The melody rises, pauses and falls back. The violins rest through its four-bar phrase and enter after it.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), II, opening four bars, printed p. 33. The four-bar opening is also described by the Munich analysis: https://openmusic.academy/docs/bmwvSwGA9xQFLhfL4GJukj/anton-bruckner-sinfonie-nr7-e-dur-wab-107
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Violins on the G string
cues.text: The violins enter on their lowest string. Bruckner keeps them on the G string as the melody climbs, marked “G Saite immer fort” in the Gutmann first edition (bars 5–9). Their five-bar phrase follows the four-bar opening.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, bars 5–9, p. 33: G Saite immer fort. Four-bar antecedent and five-bar consequent described in the Munich analysis cited above.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Remark to Felix Mottl
cues.text: Bruckner later told his former pupil Felix Mottl that he had come home one day very sad, thinking that “before long the Master would die”, and that the C♯-minor theme of the Adagio had then come to him. Wagner died in Venice on 13 February 1883.
cues.evidence: Bruckner’s remark to Felix Mottl, as given by the Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note, https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/ , and quoted by the Konzerthaus Berlin, https://www.konzerthaus.de/en/magazin/work-of-the-week-bruckner-7/217 , and the St. Louis Symphony, https://slso.org/bruckners-seventh/ . Wagner’s death in Venice on 13 February 1883: Berlin Philharmonic programme note, https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/anton-bruckner-symphony-no-7-in-e-major/

cues.title: Quotation from the Te Deum
cues.text: Twenty-two bars in, Bruckner quotes the melody he set to “Non confundar in aeternum” (“let me never be put to shame”) in his Te Deum, finished not long before. It appears once only, at a slower tempo than in the Te Deum.
cues.evidence: Analysis of the Seventh from the University of Music and Theatre Munich (Open Music Academy): the Te Deum melody is quoted 22 bars into the Adagio, once only and at a slower tempo. https://openmusic.academy/docs/bmwvSwGA9xQFLhfL4GJukj/anton-bruckner-sinfonie-nr7-e-dur-wab-107
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wagner tubas
cues.text: Wagner devised the tenor and bass tubas for his Ring. Bruckner was the first to write for them in a symphony. In this movement four of his eight horn players switch to them.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, p. 33: the page lists four horns and, apart from them, four Wagner tubas (two tenor in B♭, two bass in F) and a contrabass tuba. Konzerthaus Berlin (four of the eight horn players play Wagner tubas, for the first time, as Wagner introduced them in the Ring): https://www.konzerthaus.de/en/magazin/work-of-the-week-bruckner-7/217 . Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note (the first time another composer used them): https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/ . Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note (“the first appearance of these instruments in symphonic music”): https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-7-bruckner

cues.title: Moderato in F♯ major, strings
cues.text: The strings begin a new tune in F♯ major. The marking is Moderato, three beats to a bar, and the violins play running notes. Low strings play the bass pizzicato while clarinet and bassoon add soft phrases.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter D, p. 35: Moderato, 3/4 and pizzicato bass. Key and contrast also described by the Hungarian National Philharmonic: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Model in Beethoven’s Ninth
cues.text: Bruckner modelled this Adagio on the slow movement of Beethoven’s Ninth, in which a slow theme in 4/4 alternates with a faster one in 3/4. Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs identified the singing theme that follows the first tuba chorale as a quotation of the parallel passage in the Ninth.
cues.evidence: Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note (the alternation of 4/4 and 3/4 groups after the Ninth’s Adagio), https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/ ; St. Louis Symphony note, https://slso.org/bruckners-seventh/ ; Cohrs, Hyperion booklet note (the “Gesangsperiode” quotes the parallel section of the Ninth’s slow movement), https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: The Wagner tubas bring back the C♯-minor opening. This time the first violins play a separate line above it, and violas and cellos double the brass melody.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter G, p. 37: Tempo I, tuba melody and first-violin counterpoint.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cohrs on the Adagio as funeral march
cues.text: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs heard a funeral march in the line of those in Beethoven’s Third and Seventh Symphonies. He suggested that Bruckner may first have mourned the dead of the 1881 Ringtheater fire, and only later connected the coda with Wagner’s death.
cues.evidence: Cohrs, booklet note for the Hyperion recording of the Seventh (2023), on the Adagio as a funeral march and on the Ringtheater fire of 8 December 1881: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: Return of the tuba theme
cues.text: The tuba theme returns varied and expanded, with new countersubjects around it. The music builds to a bright outburst in G major.
cues.evidence: Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note on the returning theme, its new countersubjects and the outburst in G major: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/

cues.title: Return of the three-beat tune, A♭ major
cues.text: The three-beat tune returns in A♭ major, a whole tone above its first appearance. Flutes and oboes double the violins’ melody, and bassoons and inner strings play other moving lines. The plucked bass returns.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter P, p. 42. A♭-major return identified by the Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Third return of the tuba theme
cues.text: The tuba theme returns for the third time. Above it, the first violins play a continuous chain of arpeggios, marked to keep an even strength, without swelling. The tubas and lower strings carry the melody beneath them with crescendo markings.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter S, p. 43. In gleicher Stärke, ohne Anschwellung belongs to the first-violin line; the tubas and low strings have crescendo markings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sketch and score of the Adagio, 1883
cues.text: Bruckner finished the sketch of the Adagio on 11 January 1883. Wagner died in Venice on 13 February. By 21 April Bruckner had completed the orchestral score, and the movement, begun while Wagner was alive, ends as a memorial to him.
cues.evidence: Sketch and completion dates: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, 2023 booklet note, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D. Wagner’s death and the Adagio’s memorial ending: https://slso.org/bruckners-seventh/

cues.title: Climax in C major, letter W
cues.text: The long ascent arrives at C major. Winds and brass hold their melody across the bar, and both violin sections continue in rising and falling figures beneath it.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter W, pp. 47–48. The C-major climax is also identified by the St. Louis Symphony and Hungarian National Philharmonic programme notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cymbal crash at the climax
cues.text: The climax carries the symphony’s only cymbal crash, at its exact midpoint. Bruckner first wrote the movement without percussion and added the cymbals later. In the autograph the part is crossed out and marked “gilt nicht”, “not valid”, though the words are thought not to be his; the crash is usually played.
cues.evidence: Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note (the crossed-out cymbal part, “gilt nicht”, the prevailing view on who wrote it, the crash at the midpoint of the symphony): https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/ . Konzerthaus Berlin (cymbal and triangle inserted, deleted, marked “does not apply”; the origin of the change unclear): https://www.konzerthaus.de/en/magazin/work-of-the-week-bruckner-7/217 . Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, booklet note for the Hyperion recording (2023): the Adagio was first composed entirely without percussion, and Bruckner later added timpani, triangle and cymbals: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D . Gutmann first edition, II, letter W, p. 47: the cymbal and triangle parts at the C-major climax.

cues.title: Funeral music for Wagner, 1883
cues.text: The last thirty bars are funeral music for Wagner, who died in Venice on 13 February 1883, written “in memory of the highly blessed, dearly beloved immortal master”. Wagner tubas and horns play the closing passage.
cues.evidence: Konzerthaus Berlin (the last thirty bars, and the dedication): https://www.konzerthaus.de/en/magazin/work-of-the-week-bruckner-7/217 . Berlin Philharmonic programme note (the ‘funeral music’ and Wagner’s death): https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/anton-bruckner-symphony-no-7-in-e-major/ . Munich analysis (the Abgesang of Wagner tubas and horns): https://openmusic.academy/docs/bmwvSwGA9xQFLhfL4GJukj/anton-bruckner-sinfonie-nr7-e-dur-wab-107

cues.title: Private performance, Munich, 1885
cues.text: On the day after the Munich premiere in March 1885, Hermann Levi took Bruckner to Die Walküre. The orchestra stayed after the audience had left. Around midnight Levi had the musicians play the Adagio’s funeral music for Bruckner alone in the empty theatre.
cues.evidence: Berlin Philharmonic programme note relates the visit on the day after the Munich premiere and the private midnight performance: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/symphony-no-7-in-e-major/

cues.title: Closing chorale in C♯ major
cues.text: At letter Z the low brass hold a C♯-major chorale. Above it the horns play a fragment of the opening melody. The strings sustain the harmony, then play the last chords pizzicato.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter Z and final bars, p. 50. The brightened tonic and fragmentation of the opening are also discussed in the Munich analysis cited above.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hamburg radio, 1 May 1945
cues.text: On 1 May 1945 Reichssender Hamburg broadcast the Seventh’s Adagio after excerpts from Wagner’s Rheingold and Götterdämmerung. At 10.25 that night the music stopped, drums rolled three times, and the announcer reported Hitler’s death.
cues.evidence: Friedrich Karl Engel, “Who played Bruckner’s Adagio?”, Funkgeschichte 41 (2018), English translation by Richard L. Hess, reconstructing the Hamburg programme from the Daily Mail and Manchester Guardian of 2 May 1945: https://www.abruckner.com/down/articles/articlesEnglish/engel-friedrich-hitlers-death-as-announced-on-the-/Engel__Hitlers_Death_as_Announced_on_the_Radio.pdf

transitions.title: Clarinets descend to quiet brass chords
transitions.from: A · Wagner tubas in C♯ minor
transitions.to: Link · Clarinet and tubas without strings
transitions.how: The first orchestral crescendo ends and the strings stop. At C, two clarinets descend together above held notes in the horn and trumpet. The Wagner tubas and contrabass tuba then take over in quiet chords before the string melody that follows.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), II, letter C, p. 35.

transitions.title: Strings begin in F♯ major, 3/4
transitions.from: Link · Clarinet and tubas without strings
transitions.to: B · String theme in F♯ major, Moderato
transitions.how: The low brass diminish and stop. At D, Moderato, the metre changes from 4/4 to 3/4 and the strings introduce the F♯-major melody. Violins and violas play flowing figures over a plucked bass, and clarinet and bassoon enter as the phrase continues.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter D, p. 35. F♯ major identified by the Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note.

transitions.title: The slow tuba melody returns
transitions.from: B · String theme in F♯ major, Moderato
transitions.to: A′ · Tubas return, moving string figuration
transitions.how: The string tune slows and diminishes. At G, Tempo I restores four beats and the opening C♯-minor melody in Wagner tubas, violas and cellos. First violins play a new line above it, and horns and trumpets enter during the theme.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter G and preceding bars, p. 37.

transitions.title: The three-beat tune returns in A♭
transitions.from: A′ · Tubas return, moving string figuration
transitions.to: B′ · String theme returns in A♭
transitions.how: The orchestral passage in G major slows, grows softer and ends in a short phrase for the wind. At letter P the Moderato tempo and 3/4 time return. The tune first heard in F♯ major now begins in A♭. Flute and oboe join the violins, with figures in the bassoon below, moving lines in the inner strings and pizzicato basses.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter P, p. 42; G-major preceding passage and A♭-major return described by the Hungarian National Philharmonic.

transitions.title: Violin arpeggios under the Wagner tubas
transitions.from: B′ · String theme returns in A♭
transitions.to: A″ · Tubas beneath even violin arpeggios
transitions.how: The string phrases grow quieter and slower. At letter S, marked Tempo I, sehr langsam, the Wagner tubas bring back the C♯-minor theme over held bass notes. The first violins begin even arpeggios with an instruction against swelling. The tubas and low strings have a crescendo of their own.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter S, p. 43; distinction between the first-violin instruction and the brass dynamics.

transitions.title: Violin figures in the climb to C
transitions.from: A″ · Tubas beneath even violin arpeggios
transitions.to: C · Brass and strings in C major
transitions.how: The violin figures rise through the long crescendo while winds and brass broaden the melody. At W the orchestra reaches C major, with low C in the bass. Both violin sections continue their fast rising and falling figures beneath the sustained upper voices.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letters T–W, pp. 44–48. C-major climax identified in the St. Louis Symphony programme note.

transitions.title: Violins turn to pizzicato before tubas
transitions.from: C · Brass and strings in C major
transitions.how: After the broad C-major climax the dynamic falls. The violins change their running figures to pizzicato and the brass stop. A short woodwind phrase follows, then the strings stop as well. At letter X the Wagner tubas and contrabass tuba play their quiet, close-knit phrases alone. The strings rest throughout these opening tuba phrases.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, end of W and letter X, pp. 48–49. The strings rest throughout the opening tuba phrases at X.

transitions.title: First violins enter after the horn phrase
transitions.to: Coda · Violins after the low brass
transitions.how: The horns play an expressive phrase above the tuba chords, then diminish to pianissimo. At Y the first violins enter quietly. Violas and plucked low strings join them, followed by the flute, and the broad brass chords give way to separate string and wind lines.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, II, letter Y and preceding horn phrase, pp. 49–50.

source.title: Bruckner, Symphony No. 7, full score (Vienna: A. J. Gutmann, 1885, plate A.J.G. 576; first edition)
source.locator: II. Adagio, printed pp. 33–50; opening and letters C–D, G, N–P, S and W–Z. The horn group includes the four Wagner tubas.

timeline.note: Four Wagner tubas (played by horn players) and contrabass tuba over low strings.
Violins answer on the G string; horns and trombones enter as the phrase subsides.
The orchestra builds to the first fortissimo; trombones and contrabass tuba join the crescendo.
Clarinets descend above held horn and trumpet notes; low tubas follow without strings.
Moderato in F♯ major: a singing string theme with soft woodwind.
The C♯ minor theme returns, scored as at the start for tubas, with new countersubjects in the strings.
Winds, brass and strings join the fortissimo G-major passage.
Flutes and oboes join the A♭-major string tune; a soft horn answers.
Wagner tubas play the opening melody beneath even first-violin arpeggios.
Winds and brass reach C major above running figures in both violin sections.
Wagner tubas and contrabass tuba play alone; the strings rest.
A horn phrase rises above the tuba chords.
As the brass chords die away, the violins begin a quiet line, joined by the flute and pizzicato lower strings.

composer.epithet: Composer who studied his craft for half his life before writing symphonies in which a horn call can expand into full brass.
facts: St Florian; counterpoint with Simon Sechter, 1855–61; composition with Otto Kitzler, 1861–63
Organist at St Florian and Linz; Vienna Conservatory from 1868; university lecturer from 1875
Nine numbered symphonies, two outside the sequence; masses, motets and secular choral music
The Seventh Symphony, Leipzig, 30 December 1884; Arthur Nikisch conducting
composer.background:
On 16 December 1877 Bruckner conducted his Third Symphony with the Vienna Philharmonic. Johann Herbeck, who had intended to conduct it, had died in October. The audience began to leave during the performance. Among the supporters who stayed was the seventeen-year-old Mahler, who helped arrange the large score for piano duet. Bruckner was then fifty-three, a professor at the conservatory and an organist admired internationally. As a symphonist he was still little known in the concert hall.

He was born in Ansfelden, near Linz, where his father taught school and played church music. After his father died in 1837, his mother took him to the Augustinian abbey of St Florian as a choirboy. He learned the organ, trained as a teacher and worked in the villages of Windhaag and Kronstorf. In Windhaag he also played the fiddle for dancing.
